title: Mahajanapadas: the sixteen great states of ancient India
seo_title: 16 Mahajanapadas: List, Capitals and the Rise of Magadha
meta_description: The 16 Mahajanapadas of ancient India with their capitals in one table, plus how monarchies and ganas worked and why Magadha rose to dominate north India.
summary: The Mahajanapadas were sixteen large states in north India around the 6th to 4th centuries BCE, listed in Buddhist and Jain texts. Some were monarchies such as Magadha, Kosala and Avanti; others, like the Vajji confederacy, were ruled by assemblies. Magadha absorbed its rivals and became the base of the Nanda and Maurya empires.

paras: Mahajanapada means great janapada, a janapada being the territory where a people (jana) had settled. In the later Vedic period these were small units. By about the 6th century BCE some had grown into states with capitals, standing armies and regular taxation. Buddhist texts, especially the Anguttara Nikaya, give a standard list of sixteen; the Jain Bhagavati Sutra gives a different list, which tells us the number was a convention rather than a census.

This was also the time of the second urbanisation, the return of cities to north India about a thousand years after the Harappans. Towns such as Rajagriha, Shravasti, Kaushambi, Ujjayini and Varanasi grew, punch-marked silver coins came into use, and Northern Black Polished Ware, a glossy fine pottery, spread across the Ganga plain.

paras: Most Mahajanapadas were monarchies, ruled by a raja whose power rested on an army, a treasury and officials who collected a share of the harvest. Others were gana-sanghas, ruled by an assembly of clan heads. The Vajji confederacy, with the Lichchhavis of Vaishali as its best-known member, and the Mallas are the classic examples.

These assemblies are sometimes called republics, but that word can mislead. Power was held by a hereditary group of kshatriya families, not by all residents. Both the Buddha, from the Shakya gana, and Mahavira, from a Vajji clan, came from this world, which is one reason Buddhist and Jain texts describe it in such detail.

sections.h2: Why did Magadha become the most powerful Mahajanapada?
paras: By the 4th century BCE, Magadha had absorbed most of its rivals. Historians usually give several reasons. It controlled fertile, well-watered land in the middle Ganga plain that produced a large rice surplus. It had access to iron ore in the hills to the south. Its capitals, first Rajagriha ringed by hills and then Pataliputra at the meeting of rivers, were hard to attack. Its rulers used elephants from eastern forests in war.

Ambitious rulers did the rest. Bimbisara of the Haryanka dynasty annexed Anga and used marriage alliances. His son Ajatashatru defeated Kosala and the Vajjis. The Shishunagas ended Avanti's independence, and the Nandas built a large treasury and army. In about 321 BCE Chandragupta Maurya overthrew the last Nanda king and the [Mauryan empire](mauryan-empire.html) began.

sections.h2: Religion and ideas in the age of the Mahajanapadas
paras: The growth of cities, trade and kingdoms coincided with new questions about how to live. Alongside the Brahmanical sacrifice, teachers called shramanas left household life and wandered, debating ideas about action, rebirth and release. The Buddha (Siddhartha Gautama of the Shakya gana) and Mahavira (Vardhamana, the 24th Jain tirthankara) are the best known, but there were many others, including the Ajivikas led by Makkhali Gosala.

Their followers came from merchant families, kings and ordinary townspeople. Bimbisara and Ajatashatru of Magadha are remembered in Buddhist and Jain texts as patrons. Both traditions rejected the authority of the Vedas and the importance of sacrifice, and stressed ethical conduct. Monasteries, stupas and later cave shrines built by their communities are among the main monuments of the following centuries.

sections.h2: Seeing the age of the Mahajanapadas today
paras: Some remains survive above ground. The cyclopean wall at Rajgir is a long dry-stone fortification often linked with old Rajagriha. Kaushambi and Vaishali have excavated ramparts and stupas. Our guide to [heritage walks in Patna](heritage-walk-in-patna.html) and the Nalanda region covers the Magadhan heartland, and the [Nalanda monastic university landscape](nalanda-monastic-university-landscape.html) visit can be combined with Rajgir.

Punch-marked coins from this period are among the earliest Indian coins, and handling replicas is the quickest way to understand them: see our [introduction to numismatics with replicas](introduction-to-numismatics-with-replicas.html). For the wider sequence, read the [Indian history timeline](indian-history-timeline.html) and the guide to [major dynasties of ancient India](major-dynasties-of-ancient-india.html).

faq.a: Buddhist texts such as the Anguttara Nikaya list sixteen Mahajanapadas. Jain texts give a somewhat different list of sixteen. The number was a traditional figure, and there were other smaller states and peoples beyond those named.

faq.q: Which was the most powerful Mahajanapada?
faq.a: Magadha became the most powerful by the 4th century BCE. Before that, Kosala, Vatsa and Avanti were serious rivals. Under the Haryanka, Shishunaga and Nanda dynasties Magadha absorbed them, and it became the core of the Maurya empire.

The Vajji confederacy, centred on Vaishali, and the Mallas were gana-sanghas governed by assemblies of clan chiefs. Historians often call them republics, but power lay with a hereditary group of families rather than with all the people.

faq.q: What was the capital of Avanti?
faq.a: Avanti had two main centres: Ujjayini (Ujjain) in the north and Mahishmati in the south. It lay in the Malwa region of present-day Madhya Pradesh and was one of Magadha's main rivals before being absorbed by the Shishunagas.

faq.q: Which Mahajanapada was in the Delhi region?
faq.a: The Kuru Mahajanapada covered the Delhi area, Haryana and the upper Ganga-Yamuna Doab. Its capital is named as Indraprastha, which tradition places in Delhi near Purana Qila, where excavations have found Painted Grey Ware and later layers.

faq.q: What is the difference between a janapada and a mahajanapada?
faq.a: A janapada was the territory where a people or clan (jana) had settled, common in the later Vedic period. A mahajanapada, or great janapada, was a larger, more organised state of around the 6th to 4th centuries BCE, with a capital city, an army and regular taxation.

posts.hook: India's first cities after the Harappans rose about 2,600 years ago.
posts.caption: Historians call it the second urbanisation. Rajagriha, Shravasti, Kaushambi and Ujjayini grew into cities, and silver punch-marked coins changed how people traded.

posts.hook: Remember why Magadha won with four words: rice, iron, rivers, elephants.
posts.caption: Fertile land, iron ore to the south, capitals protected by hills and rivers, and war elephants from the eastern forests. Then add ambitious kings.
